categories.precision: Your distances are right for points far apart but wrong for points only meters apart. The arccos form (spherical law of cosines) loses precision there; the haversine form keeps it.
categories.radians: Your numbers look like sin and cos were given degrees. NumPy's sin and cos read their input as radians, so convert every angle first (np.radians).
categories.radius: Your distances are off by a constant factor close to 1. Use the sphere radius from the Contract, R = 6371.0 km, not another Earth radius.
categories.shape: Your function must take numpy arrays (or plain numbers) and give back one distance per pair, in an array of the same shape. Use numpy functions (np.sin, not math.sin) and no Python loop.
categories.units: Your distances look like meters, degrees or radians, not kilometers. The central angle is in radians; multiply it by the radius in kilometers.
categories.wrong-values: Some distances are outside the tolerance. Test by hand first: one degree along the equator is about 111.195 km, and the same point twice gives 0.

hints.1: Glossary: great_circle_distance, vectorization. The Given formula turns two latitudes and two longitudes into a central angle (the angle between the two points seen from the Earth's center); distance = radius x angle. NumPy's trigonometric functions work in radians: see the angle demo in Part 2, and Harris et al. (2020) on NumPy arrays.
hints.2: In words: convert all four angles from degrees to radians with numpy; take half of the latitude difference and half of the longitude difference; build a from the Given formula; keep a inside [0, 1] (rounding can push it a hair above 1); turn a into the central angle with arcsin and sqrt; multiply by 6371.0. Use numpy functions only, so arrays work without a loop.
hints.3:
<phi_1>, <phi_2>  :=  <the two latitudes, in radians>
<half_dphi>       :=  (<phi_2> minus <phi_1>) / 2
<half_dlambda>    :=  <(lon2 minus lon1), in radians> / 2
<a>               :=  sin^2(<half_dphi>) + cos(<phi_1>) cos(<phi_2>) sin^2(<half_dlambda>)
give back         :   <R> times 2 arcsin(sqrt(<a kept inside [0, 1]>))

hints.1: Glossary: kst, utc, time_zone. One moment can be shown on different clocks. Here you turn the same UTC moments into KST in two ways, with a fixed 9-hour offset and with the 'Asia/Seoul' time zone, and look for the rows where the two clocks show different readings. Remember Part 3: an aware time stamp is a moment; a clock reading is what a clock shows at that moment.
hints.2: In words: convert origin_utc twice with .dt.tz_convert, once to a fixed zone of nine hours (datetime.timezone with a timedelta) and once to ZoneInfo('Asia/Seoul'); write both conversions as text with .dt.strftime and the format '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S', which keeps only the clock reading; mark the rows where the two texts differ and count them; for the months, write the fixed-offset times of the marked rows with the format '%Y-%m', keep each month once and sort. Compare texts, not time stamps, and never take the month from the UTC time.
hints.3:
Why the two clocks disagree: 'Asia/Seoul' follows the time-zone database, which stores every clock
change Korea ever made. Korea used daylight saving time (summer time) in 1987 and 1988, from the
second Sunday of May to the second Sunday of October; in those weeks the zone gives UTC + 10 h,
one hour more than KST. Rows outside those weeks agree. The shape of the work (not code):
<fixed text>   :=  <origin_utc on the +9 h clock, written as a clock reading>
<zone text>    :=  <origin_utc on the 'Asia/Seoul' clock, written the same way>
<marked>       :=  <rows where <fixed text> and <zone text> are not equal>
give back      :   {'n_wrong': <how many marked rows>, 'months': <sorted distinct 'YYYY-MM' of the fixed-clock times of <marked>>}

categories.year-range: Your years do not run exactly from start_year to end_year with a count (0 when empty) for every year.

hints.1: Concept: great-circle distance (st.glossary.term("great_circle_distance")), which you met in M01. On a sphere of radius 6371 km the haversine formula is accurate enough here. Then reuse your yearly-count function.
hints.2: Plan in words: compute the distance in km from the given point to every epicenter at once with NumPy (degrees to radians first); keep the rows whose distance is at most radius_km (that is events_near); count the kept rows per year with your yearly-count function (that is counts_near).
hints.3: Shape with blanks (not runnable): distances <- <great-circle km from (lat0, lon0) to every row> ; kept <- <rows where distances <= radius_km> ; hand back <yearly counts of kept from start_year to end_year>.
